title: After Wang Fuk Court
deck: Finding a place to live after the fire
subtitle: What it takes to settle again after Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court fire.
projectNote: An independent, self-funded project for The Margins
excerpt: A ground-floor flat, a missing tenancy agreement, time to speak: accounts from the recovery at Wang Fuk Court show the practical work involved in receiving help.
cardSummary: After the fire, finding shelter was only the beginning. Public accounts show what it took to make assistance usable.

content.alt: People watching the burning towers of Wang Fuk Court at night in Tai Po, Hong Kong
content.caption: People watch the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, Hong Kong, on November 26, 2025.

content.text: Months after the fire at Wang Fuk Court, I contacted the Hong Kong Red Cross. I wanted to understand what had happened to people who had lost relatives or been forced from their homes: whether they could access financial assistance, find suitable accommodation and begin to return to everyday life. I set out these questions in an interview outline and followed up by email. This article draws on published accounts from the Red Cross and other organisations, alongside government records.

After a week in hospital, Mrs Chu needed somewhere to stay. The transitional flat was on the third floor, and her limited mobility meant she could not move in. Her husband kept looking until he found a ground-floor unit in Yuen Long. They moved there in mid-December.
Her experience appears in an account published by the Hong Kong Red Cross, which uses a pseudonym to identify her. Finding suitable accommodation was part of the work that followed her rescue.

The fire at Wang Fuk Court in Hong Kong’s Tai Po district on November 26, 2025 killed 168 people and displaced nearly 2,000 households, according to Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong. Families faced the immediate need for shelter while dealing with the loss of homes and, in many cases, loved ones.

Reading these accounts, I kept returning to the practical work involved in accepting help. An available flat has to suit the person moving into it. An application needs a way of establishing who qualifies. At a registration desk, someone may need time before they can explain what has happened.

By September, the government’s acquisition programme had reached most owners. In its September 3 update, the Housing Bureau said 1,971 owners across the estate’s eight blocks had confirmed their intention to sell their property titles, and sale-and-purchase agreements had been signed with 1,595 households as of September 2. These were milestones in acquiring the flats. The figures did not establish how many families had settled into permanent replacement homes.

The distinction matters when describing recovery. A signed agreement gives one kind of certainty. Daily life also depends on the place available in the meantime, the journeys it requires and whether ordinary tasks are manageable there. Those details deserve attention alongside the progress of a buyout.

Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong’s account of its response lists beds, wardrobes, tables, chairs, kettles and rice cookers among the items delivered to affected families. It also describes work towards a three-year housing-support programme, developed with social workers, housing operators and residents. These are ordinary household objects, but replacing them means finding the money, arranging delivery and making room in an unfamiliar space. The charity’s list gives a sense of the tasks involved in starting a household again.

content.text: Problems with emergency assistance had emerged within days of the fire. In a December 1, 2025 letter, the Hong Kong Social Workers General Union said administrative difficulties distinguishing owners from tenants had prevented some residents from receiving urgent cash relief promptly. It asked charities and other aid providers to put actual residence at the centre of their decisions.

The union also raised the possibility that identity cards or tenancy agreements had been destroyed. It urged flexibility where people could not produce complete documents, suggesting social-worker referrals or sworn declarations as possible alternatives. The letter described a concern encountered in frontline work; it did not give a total number of affected households or establish how every case was resolved.

Checking an application protects limited funds. But the evidence an organisation normally asks for may be among the things someone has lost. The union’s proposal was to make room for another way of verifying their circumstances, so that a missing document did not become the end of an application.

A volunteer’s account published on December 12 on Tzu Chi’s Jing Si website describes a different difficulty at the point of receiving help. During a visit on the first Saturday after the fire, the writer saw a distressed resident shouting at volunteers. A team leader sat with her on a bench by a park, stayed until she was calmer, and then helped her register for assistance.

That period of waiting is easy to leave out of a description of relief work. It took time that could not be fixed in advance. In this account, the volunteer made space for the resident’s distress before returning to the registration process.

Charmaine, a Red Cross psychological-support volunteer, described another strain in the organisation’s published records. Some bereaved family members told her that, when they shared their experiences with people close to them, the listeners became so upset that they needed comforting themselves. The bereaved person then had to provide that comfort.

These experiences raise a question about how assistance is organised. A household can need a decision quickly while an individual needs more time to speak. A process has to cope with both. The person at the desk, or on the end of the phone, needs enough flexibility to recognise what is being asked of them.

There are limits to what these records show. Charities select accounts to explain their work, and a few published experiences cannot stand for every household. The stories also describe particular moments after the fire. They should not be read as proof that the same difficulties remain unresolved today.

Still, they identify questions worth asking as the recovery continues. Can a resident manage the accommodation offered? Can an aid provider check an application when the usual papers are missing? Is there someone able to listen without placing another demand on the person seeking help? Answers to those questions would tell us more about how support works in practice.
For Mrs Chu, a usable home meant a ground-floor unit. Finding it took another search.
